Affairs
af-fārz'
n. pl. (business; the matters a man has in hand)
From the French à faire, to do — the things there are to do. In the Authorized Version the word covers a king's business, a province's administration, a good man's household management, and the concerns of a church for its imprisoned apostle.

Biblical Definition

“A good man sheweth favour, and lendeth: he will guide his affairs with discretion” (Psa 112:5). The psalm is an acrostic portrait of the man who feareth the LORD, and it includes his accounts. Generosity and prudence are set in one line: he lends, and he steers his business with judgment. Scripture never treats competence in ordinary matters as beneath piety. Daniel's three friends are set “over the affairs of the province of Babylon” (Dan 2:49) — and it is precisely their public competence that makes them visible when the image is set up: “There are certain Jews whom thou hast set over the affairs of the province of Babylon… these men, O king, have not regarded thee: they serve not thy gods” (Dan 3:12). Faithfulness in office is what put them in the furnace. Paul uses the word for the traffic of love between churches: Tychicus is sent “that ye also may know my affairs, and how I do” (Eph 6:21), and he longs to hear of the Philippians' affairs, “that ye stand fast in one spirit” (Php 1:27). And to Timothy the soldier's rule: “No man that warreth entangleth himself with the affairs of this life; that he may please him who hath chosen him to be a soldier” (2Ti 2:4) — not that a minister may have no ordinary business, but that he may not be tangled in it.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines affair as business of any kind, that which is done or is to be done; and in the plural, the transactions of a state or of private life.

expand to see more

AFFAIR, n. Business of any kind; that which is done, or is to be done.

1. In the plural, transactions in general; as human affairs; political or ecclesiastical affairs.

2. Matters; concerns; as, to manage one's own affairs.

DISCRETION, n. Prudence, or knowledge and prudence; that discernment which enables a person to judge critically of what is correct and proper.

Key Scripture

Psa 112:5 — "A good man sheweth favour, and lendeth: he will guide his affairs with discretion."

2Ti 2:4 — "No man that warreth entangleth himself with the affairs of this life; that he may please him who hath chosen him to be a soldier."

Dan 3:12 — "There are certain Jews whom thou hast set over the affairs of the province of Babylon, Shadrach, Meshach, and Abednego; these men, O king, have not regarded thee: they serve not thy gods, nor worship the golden image which thou hast set up."

Eph 6:21 — "But that ye also may know my affairs, and how I do, Tychicus, a beloved brother and faithful minister in the Lord, shall make known to you all things:"

Modern Corruption

Spirituality is set against competence in ordinary business; Psalm 112 puts them in one line and Daniel's friends were faithful in both.

expand to see more

A persistent piety treats attention to money, planning and administration as worldly, and treats muddle as a mark of trusting God. Psalm 112 does not agree: the man who feareth the LORD, whose seed shall be mighty upon earth, guideth his affairs with discretion. Prudence in ordinary matters is a fruit of the fear of God, not a rival to it. Deacons were appointed precisely so that a church's business would be handled by men full of the Holy Ghost and wisdom, which means the business was worth handling well.

The other side is 2 Timothy 2:4, and it is the discipline that keeps competence from becoming captivity. The soldier does not entangle himself — the picture is of a man caught in the ropes, unable to move when the order comes. Paul made tents; he was not entangled in tentmaking. Every believer, and especially every minister, has to weigh what he is holding by the question of whether he could let it go tomorrow if his Captain required it. Daniel's friends held high provincial office and walked away from all of it toward a furnace within a single afternoon.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew dabar (H1697), a word, a matter, a thing; 'abidah (Aramaic H5673), work, administration; Greek pragmateia (G4230), business, affairs.

expand to see more

Hebrew dabar (H1697) — a word, a matter, a thing done; 1 Chronicles 26:32, Psalm 112:5.

Aramaic 'abidah (H5673) — work, administration, service; Daniel 2:49, 3:12, the affairs of the province.

Greek pragmateia (G4230) — business, occupation, affair; 2 Timothy 2:4, the affairs of this life.

Greek empleko (G1707) — to entwine, to entangle; the soldier's danger — caught in ropes he cannot get free of.

Greek ta peri emou — the things concerning me; Ephesians 6:21, Philippians 1:27, Paul's idiom for news of himself.

Usage

"“He will guide his affairs with discretion” — in the psalm of the God-fearing man."

"“Set over the affairs of the province of Babylon” — and reported for it."

"“No man that warreth entangleth himself” — a soldier caught in ropes."
